ai-agent: A single, clean diagram-style illustration shows the difference between a simple chatbot and an AI agent: on the left, a small chat bubble gives one immediate answer to one question; on the right, a larger agent figure stands before a goal flag and works through a visible loop of planning, acting, checking, and revising, with icons for tools such as code, search, documents, calendars, and software APIs connected to it, while a memory panel stores past steps and notes; behind the agent, a timeline shows multiple stages of work, including drafts, error checks, retries, and intermediate outputs, and a faint swarm of smaller agents can be seen collaborating on the same task, producing many messages and traces, while a human supervisor watches from the edge with a magnifying glass and a control switch, suggesting both the power and the difficulty of auditing autonomous, multi-step AI work.
artificial-superintelligence: A single editorial illustration shows a small human figure standing beside today’s AI, depicted as a grounded but imperfect machine made of interfaces, code, training-data streams, and robotic tools, clearly powerful in narrow tasks yet still dependent on human direction. Behind it, that machine casts a vast, luminous, partly unfinished silhouette of artificial superintelligence, towering over separate scenes of scientific research, strategic planning, creative work, law, investment, public protest, and media headlines. The silhouette is rendered with dotted lines, question marks, and hazy edges to show that superintelligence remains hypothetical and contested, while bright spotlights labeled with specific achievements illuminate only fragments of it, suggesting how narrow breakthroughs can be mistaken for general superiority. In the foreground, signs and symbols of regulation, fear, funding, and present-day harm gather around the scene, making clear that the idea of superintelligence shapes real-world decisions even though no one knows whether, when, or in what form it might arrive.
frontier-ai-labs: A single panoramic editorial illustration depicts a high frontier landscape in which four rival AI laboratories, each a distinct glowing campus, stand at the edge of a cliff overlooking an uncharted world, while large general-purpose model cores emerge from them as luminous engines sending autonomous agents, code brackets, mathematical symbols, DNA strands, and robotic tools into society below. In the foreground, each lab’s team weighs testing gates, safety switches, and release doors before outputs flow outward, and those streams reach offices, research benches, courts, and government buildings, showing how frontier models automate work, assist science, and shape regulation. Around the cliff edge, the labs are also placed on adjacent racetracks, racing toward flags for capability, priority, data, and attribution, with overlapping arrows and disputed footprints suggesting competition over discoveries in mathematics, biology, and software development. The image balances bright technical progress with tense incentives, showing a few organizations building powerful general-purpose systems whose choices about testing, release, safety, and credit radiate outward to millions of users and the wider research ecosystem.
millennium-prize-problems: A single panoramic illustration depicts a dark marble amphitheater representing pure mathematics, with seven towering stone tablets or sealed doors arranged in a semicircle, each engraved with emblematic motifs for a Millennium Prize problem: prime spirals for number theory, curved surfaces for geometry and topology, quantum-like grids for mathematical physics, and especially a turbulent blue fluid vortex for the Navier–Stokes problem. Above them, a modest official banner identifies the Clay Mathematics Institute and the year 2000, while a medal or scale signifies the one-million-dollar prize. One tablet, marked as the Poincaré conjecture, is open, solved, and bathed in light, while the other six remain sealed and unresolved. In the foreground, mathematicians examine transparent, publicly displayed proof manuscripts under lenses and lanterns, showing that a solution must be rigorous, publicly available, and accepted by the mathematical community rather than merely plausible. The image presents the seven problems as famous public markers of progress in mathematics, with only one solved and accepted as of the early 2020s.
output-tokens: A single, detailed illustration shows a large language model as a luminous machine or prism at the center, receiving a document on one side and emitting a flowing stream of small labeled token blocks on the other; the blocks contain word fragments, numbers, punctuation marks, and code snippets, making clear that tokens are not simply whole words. The stream passes through a meter or gauge that measures computational effort, while tiny icons of electricity, clock time, and coins gather around it to show that output tokens represent processing load, time, energy, and cost. On the far side, the token stream forms pages of text and code, but a subtle question mark or magnifying glass hovers over the finished output, indicating that token count measures quantity and workload rather than usefulness, accuracy, or novelty.
